meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had significantly higher baseline obesity rates (BMI 25-39.9 kg/m2: 43.72% vs 34.37% in metformin users, Table 3S) and distinct sociodemographic profiles. Crucial prognostic factors (HbA1c missing in 90.52-91.79%, FPG missing in 24.13-32.95%, and BMI missing in 24.01-32.78%) were handled by matching on 'unspecified' categories rather than controlling actual values, leaving substantial residual confounding by indication and baseline metabolic severity that inflates risk estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Confounding by indication and disease severity
findings.mechanism: GLP-1 RAs are prescribed to patients with distinct diabetes progression, obesity, and treatment-resistance profiles compared to first-line metformin or late-stage insulin monotherapy. Propensity matching failed to adjust for baseline glycemic severity due to extensive missing clinical data.
evidence: Baseline HbA1c was missing for 90.52% of GLP-1 RA users, 91.79% of insulin users, and 90.45% of metformin users (Table 3S note).
Baseline FPG was missing for 32.95% of GLP-1 RA users, 32.66% of insulin users, and 24.13% of metformin users (Table 3S note).
Obesity (BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m2) at baseline was 13.21% in GLP-1 RA users vs 4.87% in metformin users and 3.04% in insulin users (Table 3S).

findings.title: Missing indicator method in propensity score matching
findings.mechanism: Matching on missingness categories ('unspecified') does not balance actual underlying continuous confounder values (e.g. 33.81% missing BMI in GLP-1 vs 36.08% in insulin matched arm), creating an illusion of balance while leaving unmeasured confounding unaddressed.
evidence: In Table 1, 33.81% of GLP-1 RA users and 36.08% of insulin users had 'unspecified' BMI; 20.53% vs 21.93% had 'unspecified' age; 33.62% vs 35.89% had 'unspecified' education.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Massive initial attrition (554,737 excluded out of 985,278, or 56.3%) due to missing IDs, missing prescriptions, and baseline exclusions creates an unrepresentative sample whose selection dynamics relative to clinical risk are uncertain.

findings.title: Massive exclusion of eligible target population
findings.mechanism: Over half of the database population was excluded due to data quality and missing records, which can induce collider stratification bias and compromise external and internal validity.
evidence: Out of 985,278 outpatients, 177,381 were excluded for missing IDs, 55,321 for prevalent baseline comorbidities, 10,139 for type 1 diabetes, and 362,035 for missing prescription data (Figure 1 and Section 2.1).

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Defining non-fatal acute symptoms (diarrhea, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia) as competing events in Fine-Gray models selectively censors or treats as competing risks the common side effects of GLP-1 RAs, distorting cumulative incidence functions for other adverse outcomes.

findings.title: Inappropriate specification of competing risks
findings.mechanism: Common, transient side effects of GLP-1 RAs (such as diarrhea/emesis, dizziness, acne) were modeled as competing risk events that terminate follow-up risk sets, rather than managing them as time-varying confounders or intercurrent events.
evidence: Section 2.3 states: 'potential competing events were systematically defined as a binomial variable, activated by any incidence of specific acute symptoms, including diarrhea/emesis, dermatitis tetter, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia, etc.'

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Complete lack of key clinical markers (over 90% missing HbA1c and >30% missing FPG and BMI) prevents adjustment for diabetes control and adiposity, directly biasing hazard ratios away from the null (e.g. sHR 3.73 for renal failure, sHR 3.20 for acute nephritis vs metformin).

findings.title: Severe missingness in core physiological and clinical variables
findings.mechanism: Without HbA1c and glycemic parameters, true baseline severity differences between GLP-1 RA, metformin, and insulin cohorts cannot be controlled, generating spurious adverse associations.
evidence: HbA1c missing rate: 90.52% in GLP-1 RAs, 91.79% in insulin, 90.45% in metformin (Table 3S note).
FPG missing rate: 32.95% in GLP-1 RAs, 32.66% in insulin, 24.13% in metformin (Table 3S note).
BMI missing rate: 32.31% in GLP-1 RAs, 32.78% in insulin, 24.01% in metformin (Table 3S).

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Patients receiving novel, high-cost injectable medications undergo closer surveillance, frequent lab testing, and specialized thyroid/pancreatic diagnostic workups compared to routine metformin users, generating detection bias that increases observed event rates in the exposed group.

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias
findings.mechanism: Outcomes such as thyroid nodules/dysfunction, asymptomatic pancreatitis, and early renal impairment are more frequently screened and diagnosed via EHR regular expressions and ICD-10 in closely monitored specialty clinic GLP-1 users.
evidence: Outcomes identified using electronic text mining regular expressions and billing ICD-10 codes without adjudication or validation (Table 2S).
Mean follow-up was 23.7 months for GLP-1 RAs, 23.2 months for insulin, and 24.8 months for metformin (Section 2.2).

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Dozens of outcomes were tested across multiple drug subgroups (liraglutide, loxenatide, lixisenatide, semaglutide) and duration thresholds (<12 vs >=12 months) without multiple testing correction, highlighting extreme positive estimates (e.g. leukemia sHR 15.09, acne sHR 5.32).

findings.title: Multiple testing and post-hoc subgroup reporting
findings.mechanism: Testing over 20 separate disease outcomes across various GLP-1 agents and duration cuts without multiplicity adjustment inflates false positive findings.
evidence: Section 3 reported numerous parallel analyses across 4 individual agents, 2 duration strata, and 2 separate comparator cohorts.
Extreme risk estimates reported for rare outcomes (e.g. leukemia sHR: 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65-48.98 vs metformin, Section 3.2).

overall.summary: This retrospective observational cohort study exhibits critical methodological deficiencies across multiple ROBINS-E domains. Confounding and missing data are at very high risk of bias due to >90% missing baseline HbA1c and >30% missing FPG/BMI, which were handled by matching on 'unspecified' missing categories rather than adjusting for actual clinical severity. Furthermore, defining treatment groups by continuous monotherapy over follow-up introduces immortal time/adherence selection bias, treating common GLP-1 side effects as competing events distorts survival models, and surveillance bias combined with unadjusted multiple testing inflates effect estimates away from the null. These flaws severely undermine the reliability of the reported adverse associations.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event counts and incidence numbers per outcome per arm (only sHRs and percentages were reported without 2x2 contingency tables).
Actual baseline glycemic control (HbA1c/FPG) and renal function (eGFR/creatinine) distributions for the >90% of participants with missing values.
Validation of EHR text-mining/ICD-10 outcome definitions against adjudicated medical chart reviews.
Frequency of clinical visits and laboratory testing per arm to quantify diagnostic surveillance bias.

baseline_comparability.summary: At baseline, GLP-1 RA users were younger but had markedly higher obesity rates, higher educational levels, and higher citizen health insurance coverage compared to metformin and insulin users. These imbalances favor increased medical surveillance and baseline metabolic risk in GLP-1 RA users, biasing effect estimates away from the null toward increased hazard of adverse outcomes.
